questions.text: Q1: Match the appropriate eye protection PPE to the hazard by writing the identifying hazard number (1–6) beneath the appropriate eye protection.
questions.hint:
Use the specific PPE questions below. Hazards:
1. Low velocity flying particles and objects
2. Medium velocity small flying particles
3. High velocity particles
4. Gas vapours
5. Non-ionising radiation only
6. Infrared and UV radiation

questions.text: For Polycarbonate face shields, which hazard number (1–6) do they best protect against?
questions.hint: Think about low velocity flying particles and objects.

questions.text: For a hood and helmet that completely seals the face, which hazard number (1–6) do they best protect against?
questions.hint: Protection against small, high-speed debris, or used in highly toxic environments.

questions.text: For wide vision goggles, which hazard number (1–6) do they best protect against?
questions.hint: Needed when working close to anyone who is creating a high velocity hazard.

questions.text: For safety glasses, which hazard number (1–6) do they best protect against?
questions.hint: Properly fitting safety glasses or goggles can help prevent injuries from dust, fumes, and vapours (Page 30).

questions.text: For safety glasses/goggles with a filter lens, which hazard number (1–6) do they best protect against?
questions.hint: Shaded safety glasses to protect your eyes from glare when brazing or using an oxy-acetylene set (Page 30).

questions.text: For a welding helmet, which hazard number (1–6) does it best protect against?
questions.hint: For arc welding, a welding helmet with the correct lenses must be worn (Page 31).

questions.text: Q2: From the photos below, select the appropriate respiratory equipment for each activity.
questions.hint: Answer the separate questions for each activity using the best respiratory protection.

questions.text: What is the most appropriate respiratory protection for sanding timber?
questions.hint: Use the extraction system and wear a dust mask over the nose and mouth (Page 35).

questions.text: What is the most appropriate respiratory protection for arc welding?
questions.hint: Wear an appropriate respirator (Page 36).

questions.text: What is the most appropriate respiratory protection for spraying glue?
questions.hint: Wear a respirator fitted with filters appropriate to the job. Dust masks are not suitable (Page 37).

questions.text: What is the most appropriate respiratory protection for spraying ‘two-pot’ paint?
questions.hint: You must wear a special breathing apparatus that has its own pure air supply (Page 37).

ASSESSMENTS.title: Learner Self-reflection 2 – 24352 (v3)
ASSESSMENTS.subtitle: US 24352 – Safe Working Practices in BCATS

questions.text: Q1: Compile a list of rules/codes of conduct that would ensure safe working practices in a BCATS environment.
questions.hint: Include rules such as: always think about possible hazards; always wear appropriate PPE; do not wear loose or dangling clothing or jewellery; tie back long hair before operating machines.

questions.text: Q1 (a–h): For each of your safety rules/codes above, describe potential consequences if they are not followed.
questions.hint: Think about consequences such as eye injuries, hair getting caught in machinery, or long-term health problems from toxic products.

questions.text: Q2: Why should jandals never be worn on a work site?
questions.hint: Think about how much protection they give compared to safety footwear (Page 50).

questions.text: Q3(a): Around heat or sparks, what type of clothing would be a hazard to wear?
questions.hint: Clothing that is not protected from heat or sparks. Overalls and a welding jacket are needed for protection (Pages 47–48).

questions.text: Q3(b): Around machinery such as lathes, what type of clothing would be a hazard to wear?
questions.hint: Machine operators should wear close-fitting clothing. Do not wear ties or baggy sleeves (Page 48).

questions.text: Q3(c): When spraying paint, what type of clothing would be a hazard to wear?
questions.hint: Spray painting requires overalls for complete body protection from paint, over-spray and chemicals (Page 49).

questions.text: Q4: Identify the potential hazards of wearing long hair around machinery.
questions.hint: If hair gets caught in a machine, it will either be ripped out or peeled from your scalp (Page 14).

questions.text: Q5: Identify the purpose of high-visibility vests or similar signage/equipment on site.
questions.hint: The purpose is to ensure that the wearer can easily be seen by plant operators to reduce the possibility of injury from moving vehicles and equipment (Page 49).

questions.text: Q6: When nailing timber you should always wear eye protection. Describe an eye hazard associated with this activity.
questions.hint: Think about flying particles or a nail ricocheting off the hammer face (Page 27).

questions.text: Q7 (General): Describe the general risk of using poorly fitting or unmaintained PPE.
questions.hint: Poorly fitting and unmaintained PPE is unlikely to protect against the identified hazard, and often exposes the wearer to additional hazards (Page 51).

questions.text: Q7(1): What are the risks of not maintaining safety glasses (e.g. not cleaning the lenses daily)?
questions.hint: Think about impaired vision and hygiene/infection risks (Page 51).

rubric.check: impaired vision|can't see|hard to see|poor visibility

questions.text: Q7(2): What are the risks of not maintaining respiratory protection (e.g. not sterilising equipment or changing filters)?
questions.hint: Think about lung diseases, cancer and other serious health-related problems (Page 52).

questions.text: Q7(3): What are the risks of not maintaining ear muffs (e.g. not cleaning or checking the pads)?
questions.hint: Think about poor fit and not getting enough hearing protection (Page 52).

questions.text: Q7(4): What are the risks of not maintaining a hard hat (e.g. not checking for cracks or splits)?
questions.hint: Think about head injuries if the hard hat fails (Page 52).

questions.text: Q7(5): What are the risks of not maintaining gloves (e.g. not checking for tears or damage)?
questions.hint: Think about chemicals or sharp edges getting through (Page 52).

questions.text: Q8(a): You are using an electric router to shape the edges of a rimu table top. Identify at least FOUR hazards and the PPE that will help protect you.
questions.hint: Think about: eye protection (particles), respiratory protection (wood dust), hearing protection (100 dB noise), body protection (loose clothing/hair), and foot protection (safety shoes).

questions.text: Q8(b): You are breaking up a concrete path using a sledge hammer. Identify at least THREE hazards and the PPE that will help protect you.
questions.hint: Think about: flying concrete chips (eye protection), impact noise (hearing protection), falling objects or tripping (foot protection), and cuts/abrasions to hands (gloves).

rubric.check: safety shoes|steel cap|falling objects|leather gloves|cuts? and abrasions?

questions.text: Q8(c): You are turning a bowl on a wood lathe. Identify at least THREE hazards and the PPE that will help protect you.
questions.hint: Think about: high velocity particles (goggles or full-face shield), wood dust (dust mask/extraction), and loose clothing or long hair (close-fitting clothing and hair tied back).

questions.text: Q8(d): You are unloading sheets of plywood off a truck and stacking them in a storage shed. Identify at least THREE hazards and the PPE or controls that will help protect you.
questions.hint: Think about: poor lifting technique (ergonomic hazard), falling sheets (foot protection), and sharp edges/coarse surfaces (hand protection).

rubric.check: poor lifting technique|back injury|ergonomic hazard|correct lifting
